faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.subtitle: Everything you need to know before taking this amazing step.

items.q: Do I need experience with cats?
items.a: No! We offer full guidance for first-time adopters. You will have all the support you need.

items.q: Can I adopt if I rent?
items.a: Yes, as long as pets are allowed and the home is safe for the cat. We help verify the conditions.

items.q: How long does the process take?
items.a: On average 3 to 7 days, depending on the match and availability. Our process is agile and humanized.

items.q: Are the cats vaccinated and neutered?
items.a: Yes! All of them undergo a complete vet check, including vaccination, neutering, and deworming prior to adoption.

facts.title: Did you know?
facts.subtitle: Fascinating information about our feline friends.

items.title: Healing purr
items.text: A cat's purr happens at a frequency (between 25 and 150 Hertz) that has been shown to improve bone density and promote healing.

items.title: Exclusive communication
items.text: Adult cats rarely meow at each other. Meowing is a communication tool developed almost exclusively to interact with humans.

items.title: Professional sleepers
items.text: Cats spend about 70% of their lives sleeping, which equates to about 13 to 16 hours a day. This preserves their hunting energy.

tips.title: First days at home
tips.subtitle: Tips to help your new friend feel safe and welcomed.

items.title: Restricted space at first
items.text: Keep the cat in a quiet room for a few days, with food, water, and a litter box, so they get used to the new smells.

items.title: Hiding spots are important
items.text: Cats feel safer when they have somewhere to hide. Cardboard boxes or 'cave' type beds are excellent for the first weeks.

items.title: Patience and space
items.text: Let the cat come to you. Forcing affection or picking them up in the first days can cause stress. Sit on the floor and wait for their curiosity.

article.title: How to introduce a new cat to other pets
article.p1: The arrival of a new feline in the house is always a moment of joy, but it requires a lot of patience and planning, especially if you already have other cats or dogs.
article.p2: Never put the animals face to face on the first day. Reserve a room in the house just for the newcomer. They will need their own litter box, water bowls, food, and places to hide.
article.p3: Before seeing each other, they should smell each other. Rub a clean towel on the new cat and place it near the food bowls of the resident animals, and vice versa. This way they will associate the other's smell with something positive (food).
article.p4: After a few days of peace, allow them to see each other through a crack in the door or a baby gate. If there are hisses or growls, close the door and try again the next day.
article.quote: The biggest mistake owners make is rushing the introduction. Feline time is very different from ours.
article.p5: When there are no longer aggressive reactions through the crack in the door, let them be in the same environment, always with supervision. Offer treats so they associate each other's presence with good times.
